blocks.text: This is a cactus. It lives where the sun is hot. It lives where rain almost never falls. The cactus has no leaves. It has sharp spines. The spines keep animals away. blocks.prompt: The Plant That Keeps Its Own Rain
blocks.text: A cactus is a plant that saves water. Most plants have wide leaves. Leaves let water escape into the air. A cactus has spines instead. Spines do not lose much water. They are really tiny leaves that changed shape long ago. The thick green stem does the job the leaves used to do. It catches sunlight and makes food. It also holds the water. Look closely and you will see folds running down the stem, like the pleats on a paper fan. When rain comes, the cactus fills with water and the folds open wide. When the water runs low, the folds close up again.

blocks.prompt: The Plant That Grows Its Own Water Tank
blocks.text: In the Sonoran Desert, rain is rare. Some years bring only a few inches of it, and months can pass with none at all. Most plants cannot live like that. The saguaro cactus can. When a storm finally arrives, the saguaro is ready. Its roots do not dig deep. They spread out sideways, just under the sand, reaching as far from the plant as the plant is tall. Rain that lands anywhere nearby gets pulled in fast, before the sun can take it back. All that water goes into the stem. The saguaro swells as it drinks. Folds along its sides open out like an accordion, letting the plant grow wider without splitting its skin. A grown saguaro can hold enough water to last through a year of drought. Then it waits. A waxy coat on the outside keeps the water from drying away. Sharp spines throw thin stripes of shade across the skin and keep thirsty animals from cutting in. The saguaro stands still in the heat, carrying its own rainstorm inside it, waiting for the next one.

notes: Cacti breathe at night, not in the day

blocks.prompt: Breathing at Night
blocks.text: Every plant faces the same trade. To make food, it must open tiny pores in its skin and let carbon dioxide in from the air. But every pore that opens also lets water out. In a rainforest that costs nothing. In a desert it can cost a plant its life. The cactus solved the problem by changing shift. During the day, when the air is hot and dry and thirsty, a cactus keeps its pores shut tight. Nothing goes in. Nothing escapes. Then, after dark, when the desert cools and the air turns still, the pores open. The cactus takes in carbon dioxide all night and locks it away inside its cells as a weak acid. At sunrise the pores close again, and the plant spends the day quietly unpacking that stored gas and turning it into food. Scientists call this trick CAM. A cactus does its breathing in the cool and its cooking in the heat, and it loses only a fraction of the water an ordinary plant would. Look closely at a cactus stem and you will find small round cushions dotted across it. These are areoles, and no other plant family has them. Every spine, every flower, every new branch grows out of one. Even so, a cactus starts life almost helpless. A saguaro seed is smaller than a pinhead, and a saguaro seedling can be cooked by one afternoon of open sun. The ones that live are usually the ones that sprout under a paloverde or a mesquite tree, sheltered by its shade. Botanists call that a nurse plant. The cactus that will still be standing in two hundred years began under somebody else's branches.

blocks.prompt: The Slow Plant and Its Twin on Another Continent
blocks.text: A saguaro keeps time badly by human standards. Plant a saguaro seed in the Sonoran Desert and come back in ten years, and you will have trouble finding it: the plant may be the size of your thumb, still hiding in the shade of the tree that sheltered it. At thirty it might reach your waist. Somewhere between fifty and a hundred years old, if it has had enough good rains, it finally pushes out its first arm. It may live past a hundred and fifty. The tall, many-armed saguaros in photographs are not simply plants. They are records of a century of weather, written one wet year at a time. That slowness is a strategy, not a failure. In a place that hands out water in rare, violent bursts and takes it back with months of drought, growing fast means growing thirsty. The saguaro spends carefully. It builds a wooden ribbed skeleton inside its stem for strength, wraps it in tissue that can swell and shrink by the ton, seals the whole thing in wax, and then simply outlasts the weather. When rain finally comes, it takes on water so quickly that a large saguaro can gain hundreds of pounds in a few days. Here is where the story widens. Travel to the dry country of southern Africa and you will meet plants that look uncannily like cacti: fat green ribbed stems, no leaves, wicked spines, the same squat barrel shape. They are not cacti. They are euphorbias, from a completely different family, and their nearest relatives include the poinsettia on a holiday table. No cactus is native to Africa apart from a single vine-like species. Africa's spiny succulents and America's cacti have never shared a desert, yet they arrived at nearly the same design. Biologists call this convergent evolution. The desert sets the exam, and unrelated plants keep handing in the same answer, because the physics leaves few options. Lose the leaves, since leaves leak. Thicken the stem, since water must go somewhere. Grow ribs, since a stem that cannot expand will split. Add spines, since a bag of water in a dry land is the most valuable thing for miles. Two families, two continents, one desert, one answer.

notes: A desert is defined by water math, not by heat
Sonoran rain arrives in two short seasons
Roots spread as wide as the plant is tall
Most of a healthy saguaro's weight is water
Flowers open at night for long-nosed bats
Woodpecker holes become elf owl nests

blocks.prompt: The Cactus Does Not Beat the Desert. It Agrees With It.
blocks.text: Consider what a desert actually is. It is not defined by heat, and it is not defined by sand. It is defined by arithmetic: a desert is any place that loses more water to the air than the sky gives back. The Sonoran Desert, which sprawls across Arizona and northwestern Mexico, may receive a dozen inches of rain in a year, and that rain does not arrive politely spread across the calendar. It comes in two short seasons, in downpours that run off the hard ground almost as fast as they land, separated by months in which nothing falls at all. Every living thing there must answer one question: what do you do with water you cannot count on? The saguaro's answer is to become a reservoir. Its roots are the first part of the argument. They do not plunge downward hunting for a water table that is not there. They radiate outward in a shallow disk, spreading roughly as far from the trunk as the plant is tall and sitting only a few inches under the surface, positioned to intercept a rainstorm in the minutes it exists. What they collect goes into the stem, which is built to inflate. Vertical pleats run the height of the plant, and as water floods in, those pleats flatten out and the whole column grows visibly thicker, the way an accordion opens. A large saguaro can put on hundreds of pounds of water in a few days, and most of the weight of a healthy one is simply water it is holding. A wooden ribbed skeleton keeps the swollen mass upright. A waxy skin keeps the treasure from evaporating. The spines, which are leaves the family gave up on long ago, break the drying wind, cast a fine mesh of shade, and make the reservoir expensive to rob. Then the plant does the hardest thing, which is nothing. It waits. Growth in this economy is a luxury purchased only in wet years. A saguaro is roughly thumb-sized at ten years old. It may not raise a single arm until it is somewhere between fifty and a hundred, and it can stand for more than a century and a half. Read that timeline correctly and a saguaro forest stops looking like scenery and starts looking like an archive. Each plant is a stack of good years and bad ones, recorded in the tissue of a living thing that had no choice but to remember them. And it does not hoard alone. A Gila woodpecker drills a chamber into a saguaro's flesh, the cactus seals the wound with a hard callus, and the woodpecker moves into the lined pocket it has made. Years later, elf owls and flycatchers inherit the room. In late spring the saguaro opens white flowers that bloom at night, when the desert is cool, and lesser long-nosed bats arrive to drink from them and carry the pollen on. Doves and bees finish the work in the morning before the flowers close for good. Every fruit is packed with a couple of thousand seeds, and nearly all of them die. The rare survivor is usually the one that lands in the shade of a paloverde or a mesquite, hidden from a sun that would kill it outright in its first summer. There is a temptation to call the cactus tough. It is the wrong word. Toughness suggests resisting the desert, and the saguaro resists nothing. It has surrendered its leaves, surrendered speed, surrendered any schedule of its own, and reorganized its entire body around the single fact that water here is rare and unpredictable. It does not beat the climate. It agrees with it, completely, and that is why it is still standing.
